content:
Tom Hales recently wrote a guest post on Terry Tao's blog. I was familiar with most of the content, but somehow had failed to "get the memo" about the gap in Mario Carneiro's thesis. Hales also joins Mario Carneiro in calling for more theoretical work to be done on Lean's type theory. A specific request concerns a relative consistency proof.

As of October, 2026, I know of no complete, public relative-consistency proof covering Lean abstract type theory. Mario Carneiro has claimed in his thesis and in lectures that there is an alternate route to establish consistency that avoids the thesis error, but to the best of my knowledge, this alternate route has never been written down, beyond a brief statement in the introduction to his thesis. In my view, a result of such fundamental importance must be given in full before it is accepted.

It seems to me that the visibility of Terry Tao's blog could help recruit some help (beyond the usual suspects) with this project, particularly if AI assistance can be of use. However, what remains unclear from Hales's blog post (and is also unclear to me) is exactly what next steps would be most helpful.

I would hazard a guess that writing down a formal specification of "what exactly is Lean 4's type theory," in a way that is robust to minor version updates, is a potential obstacle, if it hasn't been already done. This task is not completely outsourceable to AI. What is the status?

Another complication is that the arrival of con-leche (and con-ron) may create the impression that the consistency problem is solved. Hales is clear that con-leche is a major achievement, but in his opinion (and I agree) it doesn't close the book on the topic. This morning, I had a brief conversation with Jason Rute, who said that he thinks that there's too much emphasis on the question of "what Lean is" and that we should work with con-leche, rather than a formal spec, as a starting point. To me, this strikes me as akin to defining the meter as the distance between two scratches on a bar, or the kilogram as the mass of a particular hunk of metal in Paris. The latter standards served the scientific community well for decades, but were eventually abandoned when their limitations became apparent.

I recognize that I am probably re-hashing topics that have already been discussed in other Zulip threads, but again, what's new is the "What's New" blog post, which I think we can leverage to our advantage if we play our cards right. I expect that Tao would be open to a follow-up guest post that lays out more concretely exactly what help would be appreciated, in a way that might entice new people to jump in.

For anyone seeing this for the first time, earlier discussions are #general > Lean in the wild @ 💬 and #Type theory > Unique typing , the latter contains links to papers explaining the latest progress, and info on "exactly what next steps would be most helpful".

Timothy Chow said:

I had a brief conversation with Jason Rute, who said that he thinks that there's too much emphasis on the question of "what Lean is" and that we should work with con-leche, rather than a formal spec, as a starting point.

IIUC, the author of con-leche has made it very clear that the effort of con-leche is complementary to the effort of lean4lean, and the latter concerns formally specifying what Lean 4 exactly is and what properties about it can be formally proven, which is essential with or without con-leche.

Also Jason may not be wrong about the "as a starting point" part, depending on the concern and intended work. No "finishing line" is implied.

Maybe I should respond there, but a quick note. This isn’t exactly my view (and I think an honest misunderstanding by @Timothy Chow), especially the part about starting with con leche and not having a spec. I very much want a specification, but not one at the level of the type theory. I want one at the level of what kinds of theorems a Lean prover can’t prove (or more naturally, if Lean can prove phi in some restricted language, then a natural set-theoretic/categority-theoretic/type-theoretic model M should also model phi). My view is a minority view and I think the only way to convince anyone of it is to do the work myself. :smile:
Also for what it is worth, please never take anything I say about this subject as saying we shouldn’t fund type theory research in Lean. (I’m afraid I come across this way.)

@Timothy Chow said:

To me, this strikes me as akin to defining the meter as the distance between two scratches on a bar, or the kilogram as the mass of a particular hunk of metal in Paris. The latter standards served the scientific community well for decades, but were eventually abandoned when their limitations became apparent.

What in your analogy do you want the meter to be based on? Again, to be clear, for me it is certainly not con-leche. I think ZFC+{n inaccessibles | n in omega} is a good starting point that covers a lot of what we care about in Lean. (To be concrete, I think one such starting point is that if M is a model of ZFC+{n inaccessibles | n in omega} and phi is a higher-order statement of arithmetic provable in your implementation of Lean, then M |= phi. This covers completeness and much more. And unlike using con-leche as the standard, it side-steps fiddly implementation details. It doesn't cover everything, like inductives and structures, but one can do similar stuff with other restricted subsets of Lean, and also replace ZFC+{n inaccessibles | n in omega} with other very standard logical theories in set theory, category theory, and type theory.)
Jason, sorry for misunderstanding your point. As far as standards go, yes, I think that ZFC + some familiar axiom is the natural calibration.

FWIW, to continue your analogy, I believe that set theory is akin to the definition of second in terms of the Earth's rotation period: it's a valid and useful definition, but I don't want to keep it as the "official" foundation of maths forever. If, as a lot of people believe here, mechanised mathematics is to become the main user of formal mathematics, then I believe that taking whatever its foundations are as the primitive axiom system we trust is the way forward, instead of clinging to a century-old system that is not really well suited to what people want to use a foundation for these days (ie: build a proof assistant). Which does not mean we should not spend a lot of effort relating our new foundation to other, well-understood foundational systems like set theory! (In analogy, spending a lot of energy doing measurements to very precisely relate different definitions of the second was an important step to switch the official one in a way that is invisible for most people.) And this switch should happen over a long time period, likely a generation or two. But ultimately it seems strange to me that "type theory natives", who are slowly starting to appear in maths labs, would have to understand two complicated foundational systems when one is more than enough.

I'm not averse to eventually switching from set theory to type theory as the "standard" foundation for mathematics, but the type theory of Lean is still too immature theoretically IMO. As Hales says, it's pretty unsatisfactory that we can't prove unique typing. It's also not pleasant that definitional equality is undecidable. Also, it's not clear to me that we'll be able to find purely type-theoretic surrogates for large cardinal axioms (Mahlo, subtle, measurable, ...), which might become increasingly important for calibrating consistency strength. IMO, switching foundations should be done for principled reasons, rather than expediency.
Agreed! We are in the process of measuring hyperfine transitions ;)

Just a note re: unique typing: it is, in a sense, a smoking gun, for two reasons. The first is that I think it's fair to say we understand how to prove it for Lean's type theory as currently presented, only that those proofs rely on more fundamental properties which are harder to establish, and this is where the devil lies. But we are making very good progress there! The second is that this unique typing issue is a problem of one presentation (in a rather precise technical sense, the same as for group presentation): to be vaguely efficient in practical implementation, the syntax of Lean as represented in the kernel omits a lot of information, and the difficulty with unique typing is to show that what is omitted is uniquely determined by what is recorded. But there is another presentation of the type theory with all this information recorded, for which unique typing is trivial (but this is not the one we want to implement because we don't want to spend our time re-checking information we already know). You can see this sort of things at play in @Joachim Breitner's work around con-leche.
